title: Private CP upgrade runway and rollback runbook
summary: Runbook for planning, executing, and rolling back Private Control Plane (VPC/on-prem) upgrades. Focuses on Terraform module upgrade patterns, minimizing blast radius with canary rollouts, automated and manual rollbacks, KMS/HSM-aware secret rotations, and verification gates for scale and availability.
content:
Overview:
This document captures a practical, operator-friendly runbook for Private Control Plane upgrades: minor and major Terraform module migrations, control plane component image upgrades, and associated secrets/certificate rotations. It is meant for teams operating Redwood Private in VPC and on-prem environments, and assumes access to customer-approved maintenance windows and network change controls.

Scope & assumptions:
- Applies to control plane services (api-gateway, control-plane-db replicas, configstore, auth, metrics-ingest, deployment-controller) provisioned via our terraform modules.
- Target environments: customer VPCs (AWS/GCP) and on-prem racks managed by infra team.
- Operators have: terraform state access (backend), ability to SSH to bastion/jump hosts, kubectl access to control-plane clusters, and KMS/HSM console access.
- Rolling upgrades for data-plane nodes are out of scope (separate runbook).

Pre-upgrade checklist (gating items):
1) Confirm maintenance window and customer notifications posted.
2) Backup: take a snapshot of control-plane-db primary and s3 bucket export of configstore.
   - RDS snapshot / VM disk snapshot or etcd backup depending on customer infra.
3) Verify terraform state lock free and create a branch for module changes.
4) Export current hashes of module binaries, container images, and infra version tags.
5) Validate canary targets: choose 1–2 low-traffic zones/clusters for canary.
6) Health baseline: record 15m averages for request latency, error rate (5xx), token billing anomalies, queue depth, and RPS.
7) Ensure automated rollback playbooks are staged and tested in staging.

Terraform module upgrade strategy (pattern notes):
- Pattern A: Non-breaking minor bump (safe path)
  - Pin module versions for all downstream modules first.
  - terraform init -upgrade only on the module being promoted locally; run terraform plan with -out=plan.tfout and peer-review.
  - Apply to canary workspace/environment; validate; then apply to others.
- Pattern B: Structural or state-changing major bump
  - Create an intermediary compatibility branch in modules (shims) to avoid direct destructive changes.
  - Break the upgrade into N steps: 1) add new resources (side-by-side), 2) migrate traffic/config, 3) deprecate legacy resources.
  - Use state mv with careful locks only if unavoidable; prefer resource duplication plus cutover.
- Pattern C: Provider or backend changes (e.g., switch S3 backend to GCS)
  - Plan a separate migration window; export state, import into new backend in isolated environment, run smoke tests.

Canary & rollout plan (step-by-step):
1) Prepare canary workspace: terraform workspace select canary or use environment tagging.
2) Apply module changes to canary with -parallelism=2 and short timeouts.
3) Post-apply verifications (first 20 minutes):
   - API healthcheck end-to-end on a sample tenant.
   - Verify KV cache hit rate remains within baseline +/-5%.
   - Confirm no authentication failures: run token exchange tests.
4) Gradual traffic ramp for next 2 hours: shift 5%, 15%, 50% if metrics stable.
5) If any gate fails, trigger automated rollback (see rollback section).

Automated rollback triggers (examples):
- 5xx rate increased by >200% in 10m window.
- P95 latency degradation by >300ms and absolute >1200ms for 3 consecutive windows.
- Control plane queue depth >10x baseline for 5 minutes.
- Persistent failed DB migrations or >0.1% write errors.

Rollback procedures (automated + manual):
Automated (preferred):
- Our monitoring playbook will call the rollback job which:
  - marks canary nodes as draining via service discovery API,
  - triggers terraform apply to revert to previous plan (we maintain plan artifacts in S3: previous-plan-<timestamp>.tfout),
  - runs a post-rollback smoke test.
Manual (operator):
1) Halt all further terraform applies: terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> only if lock is orphaned and approved.
2) Inspect last successful plan: fetch S3 / artifacts/previous-plan-*.tfout and prepare revert apply: terraform apply "previous-plan-2025-02-09.tfout"
3) If terraform state has drifting resources, perform targeted resource replacement: terraform state list -> terraform state rm/add pattern with approvals.
4) For container image rollback: update image tags back to previous digest in deployment controller and restart pods with kubectl rollout restart deployment/<component>.

Database & migration considerations:
- No online migrations that rewrite primary keys or large table backfills during peak traffic.
- For schema changes: use additive-only migrations first; use a compatibility flag in configstore to toggle new behavior post-migration.
- If a migration fails mid-way, prefer schema rollback via backwards-compatible code path rather than forced DB schema revert.

Certificates & KMS/HSM secret rotation notes:
- Rotate TLS certs in two phases: leaf cert replacements, then CA rotation if needed.
- For KMS-backed secrets, ensure both old and new KMS keys are present for decryption during transition.
- Update key policy before rotating secrets; test decryption on a staging replica.

Scaling operations (node additions/removals):
- Scale-up plan: add nodes in the same AZ then rebalance. Allow 10–15 minutes for cache warm-up per node.
- Node drain pattern for on-prem racks: kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data <node> then wait for readiness probes.
- Horizontal autoscaler config: bump target thresholds conservatively (10–20%) to avoid oscillation after an upgrade.

Health checks and post-upgrade verification (minimal acceptance test suite):
- smoke/api-basic: POST /v1/health => 200 and payload checksum matches baseline
- auth/cookie: issue new tokens, validate claims and expiry
- controlplane-ops: list active controllers, verify leader election stability for 10 minutes
- metrics: ingest synthetic trace and ensure it arrives in observability pipeline within SLA
- billing: run token billing sample and check unit counts against expected token sizes

Emergency manual rollback (if terraform revert not viable):
- Steps: 1) cut traffic at LB level (failover to standby region or route to read-only mode), 2) restore DB snapshot to a new cluster, 3) spin up previous-version control plane using prebuilt AMIs/container digests and cached terraform outputs, 4) swap DNS and confirm.
- This path takes hours; prioritize if customer data corruption detected.

Useful commands & snippets (operator quick reference):
- terraform init -backend-config=\"bucket=redwood-tf-state\" && terraform plan -out=plan.tfout
- terraform apply \"plan.tfout\"
- terraform workspace select canary || terraform workspace new canary
- kubectl get pods -n control-plane -o wide | grep CrashLoopBackOff
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=60

Escalation & contacts:
- On-call: eng-private-deployments pager: +1-650-555-0182 -> escalates to SRE lead (Liam Chen) after 20 minutes.
- DB recovery lead: Sasha Ivanov (pager duty)
- Exec & customer comms: Product Ops (cc list in Confluence page)

Postmortem & follow-up:
- If rollback or incident occurs, create an incident in JIRA (use INF-xxxxx template), capture timelines, metric graphs, and commit SHA/terraform plan IDs.
- Add a short remediation card to the next sprint: either improve migration safety, add canary coverage, or adjust thresholds.

Appendix: blast-radius matrix (high level)
- Component: control-plane-db -> Impact: write availability, leader election -> Recovery: DB snapshot restore / promote replica
- Component: api-gateway -> Impact: request routing -> Recovery: revert image tag or failover to standby region
- Component: configstore -> Impact: feature flags and rollout configs -> Recovery: restore from s3 export and restart controllers

Notes & open questions (to resolve before GA):
- Should we add automated preflight that runs the acceptance test suite against a canary infra sandbox?
- Do we want to persist last-known-good terraform plan artifacts for all customers for 90 days? Storage cost vs recovery speed tradeoff.
- Can we treat KMS key rotation as a separate capability with a dry-run that simulates decryption across all services?

End of document.
